title: Density Estimation as Logistic Regression: NCE and What It Fathered

body:
A probabilistic model is easy to define and hard to normalise. Write down any positive function $\tilde p_\theta(x) = \exp(f_\theta(x))$ you like — a Boltzmann machine, an energy-based image model, a softmax over a million-word vocabulary — and you have a *shape* for a density. What you do not have is a density, because you cannot write down $Z(\theta) = \int \exp(f_\theta(x))\,dx$ except in textbook cases. Maximum likelihood wants $\nabla_\theta \log Z$ on every step, which is an expectation under $p_\theta$ itself; you can approximate it by MCMC, by variational bounds, or by closing your eyes and hoping, and each of those has its own failure mode. Noise-contrastive estimation, introduced by Gutmann and Hyvärinen at AISTATS 2010 and extended in their 2012 JMLR paper, gives the problem up and replaces it with a classifier.

The move is this. Introduce a noise distribution $p_n$ you can sample from and evaluate. Mix the data $x \sim p_d$ with $\nu$ noise samples $y \sim p_n$. Train a logistic classifier to say which is which. If the classifier is given the form $\sigma(\log \tilde p_\theta(u) - \log p_n(u) - \log \nu)$ and you treat the unknown normaliser $\log Z$ as a free scalar parameter $c$ absorbed into $f_\theta$, then fitting the classifier is fitting the density. You have exchanged the integral for a supervised binary task that you already know how to run.

## Why this matters now

Almost every modern self-supervised objective is a descendant of this one estimator. Word2vec's negative sampling is a simplified NCE (Mnih and Teh 2012; Mikolov et al. 2013; Dyer 2014). CPC's InfoNCE loss is an NCE over a joint distribution turned into a lower bound on mutual information (van den Oord et al. 2018). SimCLR, CLIP, and the entire contrastive-learning branch of representation learning optimise a reweighted InfoNCE. The temperature in your favourite contrastive loss is the inverse of a sampling parameter in a classifier someone trained to tell data from noise. If you cannot write down what that classifier is estimating, you cannot say what your embeddings mean. Recent theoretical work also shows the construction is more fragile than the field has treated it: the optimal noise distribution is not the data distribution, and the statistical efficiency of NCE can be exponentially bad in the ambient dimension for defensible-looking choices of $p_n$ (Chen et al. 2022; Lee et al. 2022).

## The construction, developed carefully

Let $p_d$ be the data density, which we never see directly. Let $p_n$ be a chosen noise density we can sample and evaluate pointwise. The model is a parametric family of unnormalised densities $\tilde p_\theta(x) = \exp(f_\theta(x))$. Reparametrise it by adjoining a scalar $c$:

$$\log p_m(x;\,\theta,\,c) \,=\, f_\theta(x) + c,$$

so that at the true parameters $\theta^*$, if the family is well-specified, $c^* = -\log Z(\theta^*)$ and $p_m(\cdot\,;\,\theta^*,\,c^*) = p_d$ as a proper density.

Now generate a labelled dataset of size $(1 + \nu) N$: $N$ samples from $p_d$ with label $C = 1$ and $\nu N$ samples from $p_n$ with label $C = 0$. The Bayes-optimal posterior of a uniform-prior logistic classifier over this mixture is

$$P(C=1 \mid u) \;=\; \frac{p_d(u)}{p_d(u) + \nu\, p_n(u)} \;=\; \sigma\!\left(\log\frac{p_d(u)}{p_n(u)} - \log\nu\right),$$

where $\sigma$ is the logistic. Replace $p_d$ with the model $p_m(\cdot\,;\,\theta,\,c)$ inside the sigmoid and you have a classifier *parametrised by the density*. The NCE objective is the expected log-likelihood of that classifier,

$$J(\theta, c) \,=\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_d}\!\left[\log \sigma(G_{\theta,c}(x))\right] \;+\; \nu\, \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_n}\!\left[\log(1 - \sigma(G_{\theta,c}(y)))\right],$$

$$G_{\theta,c}(u) \;=\; f_\theta(u) + c - \log p_n(u) - \log\nu.$$

Maximise $J$ over $(\theta, c)$. Gutmann and Hyvärinen's main theorem (2012) states that if $p_n$ is strictly positive wherever $p_d$ is, and the extended family is identifiable, then the empirical maximiser converges in probability to $(\theta^*, c^*)$ as $N \to \infty$, and asymptotically the estimator is normal with a computable sandwich variance. Consistency holds for any $\nu \ge 1$; efficiency improves as $\nu$ grows, and in the limit $\nu \to \infty$ NCE recovers the maximum-likelihood asymptotic variance. None of this requires computing $Z$.

The identity in that sandwich is worth dwelling on. The classifier cannot be solved by cheating with a large $c$: if $c$ pushes $p_m$ up everywhere, the second term of $J$ punishes it in regions where noise dominates. The two terms balance exactly at $c = -\log Z(\theta)$. That is why the normaliser becomes a free parameter you *recover* instead of an integral you have to *compute*. The partition function was never a thing to calculate; it was a classifier's bias term.

## Negative sampling is not quite NCE

Mikolov et al.'s skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) reads, for a word $w$ and a context $c$,

$$\ell_{\text{SGNS}} \;=\; \log \sigma(v_w^\top u_c) \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}_{w_k \sim p_n}\!\left[\log \sigma(-v_{w_k}^\top u_c)\right].$$

This is *almost* NCE's binary logistic likelihood with $\nu = K$, except that the argument of $\sigma$ is $v_w^\top u_c$, not $v_w^\top u_c - \log p_n(w) - \log K$. Dyer's 2014 note made the consequence precise. NCE's logistic is calibrated so that its Bayes-optimal solution equals $\log(p_d / p_n) - \log \nu$; SGNS's logistic has no such calibration, and its Bayes-optimal $v_w^\top u_c$ at the population level equals $\log(p_d / p_n)$ only when $\nu\, p_n(w)$ is uniform in $w$ — which it is not for word frequencies. SGNS is therefore a *representation learner* that happens to use the same binary loss, not a density estimator. Levy and Goldberg (2014) finished the story by showing the SGNS solution implicitly factorises a shifted pointwise mutual information matrix. Treating it as an unbiased MLE for a language model will give you miscalibrated probabilities; using it to make word vectors is a different task.

## InfoNCE as NCE over a joint

Van den Oord et al.'s Contrastive Predictive Coding puts NCE into the joint between two views of the data. Given $N$ paired samples $(x_i, y_i) \sim p(x,y)$, pick one positive pair $(x_1, y_1)$ and treat the other $y_i$ as negatives sampled from the marginal $p(y)$. With a score $f(x,y)$, the InfoNCE loss is

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log \frac{f(x_1, y_1)}{\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_1, y_i)}\right].$$

At the population optimum, $f^*(x,y) \propto p(y\mid x)/p(y)$, which is the pointwise density ratio NCE was estimating in the first place — only now the "noise" is the marginal $p(y)$ and the "data" is the joint. From that stationary point one derives the bound

$$I(X;Y) \;\ge\; \log N - \mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}},$$

so minimising InfoNCE maximises a lower bound on mutual information. Two facts about this bound are worth internalising. It is capped at $\log N$: regardless of how good the model is, you cannot certify more MI than the logarithm of your batch size. And it is the *tightest* NCE-style MI bound at that budget. If someone tells you their representations have 20 nats of mutual information with the label but their batch size is 256, they are telling you nothing — the bound saturates at 5.5.

## A concrete anchor

A toy implementation of NCE on a one-dimensional unnormalised Gaussian is short enough to read, and it makes the role of $c$ and $\nu$ visible:

```python
import math, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# data: N(2, 1); noise: N(0, 2); model: exp(a*x + b*x^2 + c)
mu_d, sd_d = 2.0, 1.0
mu_n, sd_n = 0.0, 2.0
params = torch.zeros(3, requires_grad=True)   # a, b, c
opt = torch.optim.Adam([params], lr=5e-3)

def log_pm(x, p):
    return p[0] * x + p[1] * x**2 + p[2]

def log_pn(x):
    return -0.5 * ((x - mu_n) / sd_n)**2 - math.log(sd_n * (2 * math.pi) ** 0.5)

nu, N = 5, 4096
for step in range(4000):
    x = mu_d + sd_d * torch.randn(N)
    y = mu_n + sd_n * torch.randn(nu * N)
    g_x = log_pm(x, params) - log_pn(x) - math.log(nu)
    g_y = log_pm(y, params) - log_pn(y) - math.log(nu)
    loss = -(F.logsigmoid(g_x).mean() + nu * F.logsigmoid(-g_y).mean())
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
# params -> a ≈ 2, b ≈ -0.5, c ≈ -log Z_data
```

At convergence the recovered $a, b$ encode the mean and variance of the data Gaussian ($a = \mu_d / \sigma_d^2 = 2$, $b = -1/(2\sigma_d^2) = -0.5$), and $c$ equals $-\log Z$ for that Gaussian — no integral evaluated. Change $\nu$ and the asymptotic variance of each parameter moves with it in the pattern the 2012 paper predicts; change $p_n$ to concentrate near the data mean and it collapses, because the classifier never has to distinguish anything in the tails and the Fisher information at $\theta^*$ goes with it.

## What it implies in practice

Three habits worth keeping. First, when you need a density and the normaliser is intractable, reach for a classifier before you reach for MCMC. NCE's statistical efficiency is worse than MLE but its optimisation is much better behaved — you train a stable supervised objective instead of alternating between a sampler and a gradient. Second, when you reach for a contrastive loss, know which version you have. SGNS-style losses are representation learners with no density guarantee; NCE and InfoNCE are density-ratio estimators with one. If you need calibrated probabilities you must use the calibrated form. Third, treat the noise distribution as a hyperparameter with teeth. The common instinct is to make $p_n$ resemble $p_d$, on the folk theory that "hard negatives" are informative. The 2022 analysis by Chen, Risteski and collaborators shows this intuition is wrong in the asymptotic-variance sense: the optimal noise is biased toward low-density regions of the data, and matching $p_n$ to $p_d$ can be strictly suboptimal. Lee, Pabbaraju, Sevekari, and Risteski (2022) sharpen the warning for high-dimensional energy-based models: a Gaussian noise matched to the data covariance can give an NCE Hessian whose condition number is exponential in $d$, destroying any hope of a sensible rate.

## Limits and open questions

The consistency theorem assumes that $p_n > 0$ wherever $p_d > 0$. In practice, data in high dimensions lives on low-dimensional manifolds, and any smooth $p_n$ assigns essentially zero mass to the data manifold. "Essentially zero" is still formally positive, so consistency as a statement about $N \to \infty$ holds, but the effective sample size needed for finite-sample accuracy may be astronomical. This is the sense in which NCE "works in theory and not in practice" for image models — and is also why diffusion-style score matching has eclipsed NCE in the generative-modelling frontier, since score matching does not need the support-coverage assumption at all.

Negative sampling's lack of a consistency guarantee is not a disaster for representation learning: the matrix Levy and Goldberg identified is a sensible target in its own right. But it is a reason not to compose SGNS vectors with downstream probabilistic machinery that assumes calibrated log-probabilities. The practice of using contrastive logits as "scores" is pervasive and mostly fine, but the step from "score" to "probability" is a step where the derivation should be checked, not assumed.

InfoNCE's $\log N$ cap is a structural, not a statistical, limit — no amount of data lifts it — and the common practice of quoting an InfoNCE value as if it were an estimate of mutual information remains a category error that the critique literature has been pointing out since 2019. It is a bound. A tight bound is a measurement; a loose bound saturated at its ceiling is a hyperparameter.

Finally, the choice of noise distribution is an under-specified corner of modern practice. The theoretical optima known so far are available only in idealised regimes — exponential families, Gaussian data — and the general case is open. For most practitioners this means that *reporting the noise distribution and the negative count is part of reporting the method*, and that a contrastive result that does not survive a change in $p_n$ was never about $p_d$ in the first place.

## Further reading

- Michael Gutmann and Aapo Hyvärinen, *Noise-contrastive estimation: A new estimation principle for unnormalized statistical models*, AISTATS 2010, PMLR 9:297–304. <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/gutmann10a.html>. The original paper. Short and self-contained; read Sections 2–3 for the construction, Section 4 for the consistency argument.
- Michael Gutmann and Aapo Hyvärinen, *Noise-Contrastive Estimation of Unnormalized Statistical Models, with Applications to Natural Image Statistics*, JMLR 13:307–361, 2012. <https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v13/gutmann12a.html>. The extended version with full asymptotic theory, the sandwich variance, and the image-model experiments.
- Andriy Mnih and Yee Whye Teh, *A Fast and Simple Algorithm for Training Neural Probabilistic Language Models*, ICML 2012. <https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~teh/research/compling/MniTeh2012a-poster.pdf>. Applies NCE to neural language modelling and introduces the self-normalisation trick ($Z_c = 1$) that most later NLP work inherited.
- Tomas Mikolov, Ilya Sutskever, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, and Jeff Dean, *Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality*, NeurIPS 2013; arXiv:1310.4546. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546>. The skip-gram negative sampling paper. Read with Dyer's note alongside.
- Chris Dyer, *Notes on Noise Contrastive Estimation and Negative Sampling*, arXiv:1410.8251, 2014. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8251>. Four pages that settle the question of what SGNS is and is not. The right thing to hand to a student who thinks they already understand the distinction.
- Omer Levy and Yoav Goldberg, *Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization*, NeurIPS 2014. <https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5477-neural-word-embedding-as-implicit-matrix-factorization>. Identifies the shifted-PMI matrix that SGNS factorises; the companion to Dyer's note on the representation-learning side.
- Aaron van den Oord, Yazhe Li, and Oriol Vinyals, *Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding*, arXiv:1807.03748, 2018. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03748>. Introduces InfoNCE and the $\log N$ mutual-information bound. Reads in an afternoon.
- Omar Chehab, Aapo Hyvärinen, and Andrej Risteski, *The Optimal Noise in Noise-Contrastive Learning Is Not What You Think*, arXiv:2203.01110, 2022. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01110>. Derives the asymptotic-MSE-optimal noise distribution and shows it is systematically different from the data distribution. Good as a counterweight to the "harder is better" folk theory.
- Holden Lee, Chirag Pabbaraju, Anish Sevekari, and Andrej Risteski, *Pitfalls of Gaussian Likelihoods for Fitting Models to High-Dimensional Data (and NCE)*, arXiv:2210.00189, 2022. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.00189>. The worst-case bound for the default Gaussian-noise choice: condition number exponential in dimension.
